{{nihongo|'''Hioki Shrine (Nagoya)'''|日置神社 (名古屋市)}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} in Tachibana 1-chōme, {{ill|Naka-ku, Nagoya|Q1207921|qid=Q1207921|lt=Naka Ward}}, {{ill|Nagoya|Q11751|qid=Q11751}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|Q80434|qid=Q80434}}. It is also called "Hioki Hachimangū." It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} identified with "Hioki Shrine" of Aichi District, Owari Province, in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932}}. {{nihongo|'''Hioki Shrine (Nagoya)'''|日置神社 (名古屋市)}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Owari Province]].

== Enshrined deities ==
* {{ill|Futodama|qid=Q11059539|lt=Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto}} (あめのふとだまのみこと)
* Left co-enshrined deity: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Homuda-wake-no-Mikoto}} (ほむだわけのみこと)
* Right co-enshrined deity: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amaterasu Kōtaijin}} (あまてらすすめおほかみ)

== History ==
Foundation is unknown. Until the early modern period it was called '''Hachimangū''' and was the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}} of Hioki village in Aichi District. In the mid-Edo period, {{ill|Amano Sadakage|Q6535030|qid=Q6535030}} identified this shrine with the "Hioki Shrine" of the Engishiki Jinmyōchō because it was located in Hioki village, and this became accepted theory. There are no differing theories identifying this shrine as Hioki Shrine; even late-Edo scholar {{ill|Tsuda Masanari|Q22123474|qid=Q22123474}} regarded it as Hioki Shrine.

A wooden tablet has been excavated from {{ill|Heijō-kyō|Q862509|qid=Q862509}} bearing the text "Hioki-ri, Kusabe-gō, Aichi District, Owari Province," suggesting this area was called "Hioki-ri" in the {{ill|Nara period|af|Nara-tydperk|ar|فترة نارا|bcl|Panahon nin Nara|bg|Нара (период)|bn|নারা যুগ|ca|Període Nara|ckb|سەردەمی نارا|cs|Období Nara|de|Nara-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Νάρα|eo|Epoko de Nara|es|Período Nara|eu|Nara aroa|fa|دوره نارا|fi|Nara-kausi|fr|Époque de Nara|gl|Período Nara|he|תקופת נארה|hr|Nara (razdoblje)|hu|Nara-kor|id|Zaman Nara|it|Periodo Nara|ja|奈良時代|jv|Periodhe Nara|ko|나라 시대|lt|Nara laikotarpis|ml|നാറ കാലഘട്ടം|ms|Zaman Nara|nl|Naraperiode|nn|Naratida|no|Nara-perioden|oc|Periòde de Nara|pl|Nara (okres)|ps|نارا|pt|Período Nara|ro|Perioada Nara|ru|Период Нара|sh|Nara period|simple|Nara period|sk|Obdobie Nara|sl|Obdobje Nara|sr|Нара период|sv|Naraperioden|th|ยุคนาระ|tl|Panahong Nara|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Nala|tr|Nara Dönemi|uk|Період Нара|ur|نارا دور|vi|Thời kỳ Nara|war|Panahon Nara|wuu|奈良时代|zh|奈良時代|zh_min_nan|Nara sî-tāi|zh_yue|奈良時代|qid=Q189178}}. The name "Hioki" has many unclear points, but one theory derives it from the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hioki-be}} who managed calendars. Around the shrine, several ancient sites are confirmed, including the {{ill|Ōsu Kofun Group|Q133820892|qid=Q133820892}} and {{ill|Hatagochō archaeological site|Q30926880|qid=Q30926880|lt=Hatagochō archaeological site}}. For divine rank, the Atsuta manuscript of the {{ill|Owari Kokunai Jinmyōchō|Q11041830|qid=Q11041830}} lists "Junior First Rank Upper, Hioki Tenjin," while the Kōnomiya manuscript has "Junior Third Rank, Hioki Tenjin."

In the medieval period, it is said Hachiman Ōkami was invited from Otokoyama in {{ill|Yamashiro Province|Q749276|qid=Q749276}} and jointly enshrined (possibly also connected to {{ill|Wakamiya Hachiman-gū Shrine (Kyoto)|Q11616253|qid=Q11616253}} at Kyoto Higashiyama Gojō). In the fifth month of {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}} 3 ({{ill|1560|Q6613|qid=Q6613}}), when {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|Q171411|qid=Q171411}} departed for the {{ill|Battle of Okehazama|Q349422|qid=Q349422}}, he left Kiyosu Castle at dawn, came to this shrine, performed "Atsumori" and prayed for victory, then moved to {{ill|Atsuta Shrine|Q482065|qid=Q482065}} after his forces assembled. After his victory, he planted one thousand pine trees in the sacred precinct as thanksgiving; since then it was called "Senbonmatsu Hioki Hachimangū."

Until before WWII, the shrine possessed munafuda with dates such as {{ill|Bunroku|Q1373039|qid=Q1373039}} 1 ({{ill|1592|Q6769|qid=Q6769}}) and {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}} 13 ({{ill|1608|Q6758|qid=Q6758}}), indicating multiple rebuilding phases from Sengoku through Edo. The early-Edo ''{{ill|Kanbunmuramuraoboegaki|Q137766629|qid=Q137766629}}'' records "Hioki village... Hachiman ... Atsuta negi Oritaifu ... exempt from before," showing it was under Atsuta negi Ōhara Oritaifu. The nearby Shichimenzan Myōzen-ji appears to have been built by carving out shrine land; records remain of annual land-tax payments as ground rent to Ōhara Oritaifu.

At the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707}}, the shrine name was changed to "Hioki Shrine." In {{ill|1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746}} ({{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 4), it was promoted to gōsha. During {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ca|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-Bunri|es|Shinbutsu bunri|fa|شینبوتسو بونری|fi|Shinbutsu bunri|fr|Shinbutsu bunri|id|Shinbutsu bunri|it|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|ru|Симбуцу бунри|tr|Şinbutsu-bunri|zh|神佛分離|qid=Q1970535}}, shrine families resigned with source materials, resulting in dispersal of records. In {{ill|1896|Q7846|qid=Q7846}} (Meiji 29), the last of the thousand pines reportedly died. On Dec 26, {{ill|1907|Q2048|qid=Q2048}} (Meiji 40), it was designated a shinsen-heihaku-ryō kyōshin shrine. In Oct {{ill|1909|Q2057|qid=Q2057}} (Meiji 42), neighboring village Shinmei-sha was merged and co-enshrined. In Mar {{ill|1945|Q5240|qid=Q5240}} (Shōwa 20), it was damaged in the {{ill|Bombing of Nagoya|Q2813858|qid=Q2813858}}. In {{ill|1958|Q5253|qid=Q5253}} (Shōwa 33), restoration and rebuilding of shrine buildings was completed.
